candidates.explanation: The LanguageManager class is marked as @unchecked Sendable, which bypasses the compiler's data race safety checks. While the code uses an NSLock to manage access to _current, using @unchecked Sendable manually overrides the safety guarantees provided by Swift's concurrency model.
candidates.title: Use of @unchecked Sendable

evidence.description: The LanguageManager uses NSLock to synchronize access to the _current Language property.

candidates.explanation: The use of NSLock in a global singleton manager for a simple enum value can lead to contention in high-concurrency environments. Furthermore, using a lock to protect a single property can be less efficient than using an Actor or a thread-safe atomic wrapper.
candidates.title: Potential for Deadlock or Performance Bottleneck with NSLock

evidence.description: /// Note: Since Language is Sendable (simple enum), direct static var access is safe
public static var current: Language { get { LanguageManager.shared.unsafeCurrent } set { LanguageManager.shared.unsafeCurrent = newValue } }

candidates.explanation: The comment on line 18 claims that direct static var access is safe because Language is a simple enum, but the implementation actually routes all access through a manual locking mechanism in LanguageManager, creating a contradiction between the documentation and the implementation.
candidates.title: Inconsistent Thread-Safety Documentation
